10140:
A malformation is an abnormal or irregular structure in something — most often a body part or organ — that came about because it did not develop or form the way it was supposed to. It is the physical result of something going wrong during the process of forming or growing. Think of it this way: when a structure is built or grows incorrectly, the flawed result is called a malformation.

The word always refers to a thing — a noun — meaning it points to the actual abnormal structure itself, not the process of it happening.

There are two ideas fused together in this word:

"Bad or wrong" + "the way something was formed or shaped" = a structure that formed badly or wrongly.

The critical word here is formed. A malformation is not just any problem. It is specifically a problem with structure — with the shape, arrangement, or physical construction of something. A malformation is not about how something behaves or functions (that would be a dysfunction). It is about how something is physically built or shaped.

That said, a malformation very often causes a dysfunction, because when something is built wrong, it usually does not work right either.

Here is the key checklist:

  • The structure exists in a form that is different from its normal, expected shape or arrangement.
  • This difference arose because the structure did not develop correctly — it was not formed right, right from the beginning.
  • It is not a result of injury or damage to something that was previously normal. If a bone breaks, that is not a malformation. But if a bone grew in the wrong shape from the start, that is a malformation.
  • The term usually implies a significant deviation from normal — not just a tiny variation, but something noticeably or meaningfully wrong.
Where Is This Word Used Most?

In Medicine (the most common context)

Malformation is used most heavily in medicine, especially when talking about the human body — particularly structures that did not develop correctly before or around birth.

Examples:

  • A heart malformation means the heart or one of its chambers, valves, or blood vessels did not form in the right shape. This is one of the most common types of birth defects.
  • A brain malformation means a part of the brain has an abnormal structure — for example, the two halves of the brain may not have separated properly, or a part of the brain may be missing or misshapen.
  • A skeletal malformation might mean a limb, a rib, or the spine has developed in an unusual or incorrect shape.
  • A vascular malformation refers to an abnormal formation of blood vessels — for instance, blood vessels that are tangled, oversized, or connected in a way they should not be.

The phrase congenital malformation is extremely common. "Congenital" means "present at birth," so a congenital malformation is an abnormal structure that a person is born with, having developed wrongly in the womb.

In Nature and Biology (outside the human body)

The word is not limited to human medicine. It also applies to animals and plants:

  • A bird born with a wing that did not grow into the correct shape has a wing malformation.
  • A plant that develops a stem or leaf in an abnormal structural form can be said to have a malformation.

In Engineering and Architecture (less common, but used)

Though rare, you can technically use malformation when describing non-living structures. A structure that was physically built or formed incorrectly — especially in a way that deviates significantly from its intended design — can be referred to as a malformation. However, in this context, people more often use words like "defect," "flaw," or "structural fault."

Malformations are not all equally serious. They exist on a wide spectrum:

  • Minor malformations — small structural differences that cause no major problems and may even go unnoticed. For example, a minor malformation of a toe that causes no pain or difficulty.
  • Major malformations — significant structural abnormalities that affect how a body part or organ functions, and may require medical treatment, surgery, or lifelong management. A serious heart or brain malformation would fall here.

While you did not ask for this, understanding causes gives the word much more meaning:

  • Genetic factors — errors or variations in a person's genes can cause structures to form incorrectly during development.
  • Environmental factors during development — exposure to harmful substances, infections, radiation, or certain medications during pregnancy can interfere with how a baby's structures develop.
  • Unknown causes — in many cases, doctors cannot pinpoint an exact reason why a malformation occurred.
  • Random developmental errors — sometimes, the complex biological process of forming a structure simply goes wrong by chance.
How Is This Word Used in Sentences?

Here are natural, realistic examples:

  • "The baby was born with a malformation of the heart that required surgery shortly after birth."
  • "The scan revealed a malformation in the brain that had likely been present since before birth."
  • "The surgeon specializes in correcting malformations of the spine in children."
  • "The colt had a leg malformation that prevented it from walking normally."
  • "Doctors discovered the malformation during a routine ultrasound in the third month of pregnancy."
  • "Not all malformations are visible from the outside — many are internal structural differences."
  • "The patient lived a full life despite the minor malformation found in her kidney."

Understanding nearby words will sharpen your understanding:

Malformed (adjective) — This is the describing form of the word. It describes something that has a malformation. "The child was born with a malformed ear."

Deformity — Very close in meaning, and often used interchangeably in everyday speech. However, strictly speaking, deformity tends to suggest a distortion or disfigurement — something bent, twisted, or warped out of its normal shape. Malformation specifically emphasizes that the structure was never formed correctly in the first place. In practice, especially in medicine, the two words often overlap significantly.

Anomaly — A broader word meaning simply "something that is unusual or different from normal." A malformation is a type of anomaly, but an anomaly does not have to be a malformation. An anomaly could be something unexpected in behavior, results, or data — not just physical structure.

Abnormality — Also a broader word meaning anything that deviates from the normal. A malformation is a physical structural abnormality, but not every abnormality is a malformation.

Defect — A very common synonym in medical and everyday usage. "Birth defect" and "congenital malformation" are often used to describe the same thing. However, "defect" has a slightly more general sense — it can refer to any kind of flaw (including functional flaws), while "malformation" is specifically structural.

A malformation is a physical structure — usually a body part or organ — that has an abnormal shape or form because it did not develop correctly. It is the name for the wrongly formed structure itself. The word is most at home in medical and biological contexts, particularly when discussing structures that were built incorrectly from the very beginning of their development. It differs from injury (which damages something that was once normal) and dysfunction (which is about performance, not shape). Malformations range from minor to life-altering, and they can affect any structure in a living thing.
10141:
A malfunction is when something stops working the way it is supposed to work.

More precisely: it is an instance of a device, system, machine, organ, or process operating incorrectly, improperly, or not at all — in a way that is different from how it was designed or expected to behave.

The word carries a built-in assumption: there is a correct, intended way this thing should work, and a malfunction is a departure from that. You cannot say a rock "malfunctioned." But you can say a rocket's engine did, because the engine was built with a specific, expected purpose.

A malfunction can take several forms:

  • Partial failure: The thing still works, but not fully or correctly. A keyboard malfunction where some keys stop responding is still a malfunction — the keyboard hasn't gone completely dead, but it no longer does its job properly.
  • Complete failure: The thing stops working entirely. A total power system malfunction leaves everything it was powering dark and dead.
  • Unpredictable behavior: The thing does something, but not what it is supposed to. A software malfunction might cause a program to open a wrong file, crash suddenly, or display scrambled data — it is "doing something," but doing it wrong.

The word applies across a wide range of domains:

Machines and technology: An engine malfunction, a sensor malfunction, a computer malfunction, a brake malfunction. These are perhaps the most common uses.

Software and digital systems: A software malfunction, a system malfunction, a navigation malfunction. Here it means the code or system is behaving incorrectly.

Biological systems and organs: A kidney malfunction, a thyroid malfunction, a heart malfunction. In medicine, it is used when an organ is not performing its biological role correctly — secreting the wrong amount of a hormone, filtering blood poorly, etc.

Processes and mechanisms: Even broader systems — like a safety protocol, a communication network, or an automated factory process — can experience a malfunction if they deviate from their designed operation.

A malfunction sits in the middle-to-serious range of severity, but it does not always mean total destruction. Think of it as a spectrum:

  • A minor malfunction: a small, perhaps temporary deviation. A flickering screen, a door sensor that sometimes fails to detect movement.
  • A serious malfunction: significant and potentially dangerous departure from normal function. A brake malfunction on a car. A reactor cooling system malfunction.

The word itself does not tell you exactly how bad things are — context does. But using "malfunction" signals that the problem is real and meaningful, not just a trivial inconvenience.
How to Use It in a Sentence

"The spacecraft experienced a malfunction in its navigation system, forcing mission controllers to take manual control."

"Doctors discovered a malfunction in the patient's immune system that was allowing infections to go undetected."

"A malfunction in the factory's assembly line caused production to halt for six hours."

"The pilot reported a malfunction before the emergency landing."

Notice the common verbs that pair with malfunction:

  • experience a malfunction
  • report a malfunction
  • cause a malfunction
  • suffer a malfunction
  • detect / discover a malfunction

And the common adjectives:

  • technical malfunction
  • mechanical malfunction
  • software malfunction
  • equipment malfunction
  • system malfunction
  • minor / major malfunction
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, but each has its own shade of meaning:

Malfunction vs. failure
A failure is often more absolute — it suggests something has completely stopped working or has collapsed entirely. A malfunction can be partial; the thing is misbehaving but may still be running in some form. A "heart failure" is a graver, more catastrophic event than a "heart malfunction," even though both are serious. In everyday use, though, they often overlap.

Malfunction vs. glitch
A glitch is typically minor and temporary — a brief, small hiccup that fixes itself or is easily corrected. A malfunction implies something more substantial and lasting. You would say your phone had a glitch if it froze for two seconds; you would say it had a malfunction if it can no longer make calls.

Malfunction vs. defect
A defect is a flaw that exists from the beginning — usually from the manufacturing or design stage. A malfunction can happen at any point in a device's life, including after it has been working correctly for years.

Malfunction vs. breakdown
A breakdown almost always implies complete, total cessation of function — the car broke down, meaning it stopped running entirely. A malfunction can be either partial or total, making it the broader of the two terms.

Malfunction vs. error
An error often refers to a mistake made by a person, or a specific incorrect value or action in a system. A malfunction refers to the broader failure of the system or device itself to operate correctly. Your GPS app might show an error (a wrong data point), but if the whole app freezes and cannot be used, that's a malfunction.

"Malfunction" is a fairly formal, technical-sounding word. You are more likely to see it in engineering reports, medical documents, news articles about accidents, official statements, and technical manuals than in casual conversation. When it appears, it signals seriousness — that something has gone wrong in a way worth investigating and correcting. It is a neutral, factual word; it describes a problem without assigning blame.

A malfunction (noun) is a specific occurrence of something — a machine, system, organ, or process — failing to work as it is designed or expected to. It can be partial or total, temporary or lasting, and spans everything from a faulty keyboard key to a failing human organ to a spacecraft navigation failure. It implies a known standard of correct operation, against which the failure is measured.
10142:
Malice is the desire to cause harm, pain, or suffering to someone — and crucially, doing so on purpose, with full awareness and intention.

It is not an accident. It is not a moment of rage. It is a cold, deliberate wish to see someone hurt, damaged, or destroyed. When someone acts with malice, they are not just angry — they want bad things to happen to a specific person (or people), and they may take steps to make that happen.

Think of it this way: if a rock falls and hits you, that's an accident. If someone throws a rock at you in a blind, unthinking fury, that might be anger. But if someone carefully plans to drop a rock on you at exactly the right moment because they want you to suffer — that is malice.

Malice always contains two things working together:

  1. Intent — the person means to cause harm. It is a choice, not a slip.
  2. Ill will — there is a hostile, negative feeling toward the target. They want the person to suffer, not just that they don't care whether the person suffers.

Both must be present. A surgeon who accidentally injures a patient has neither. A driver who runs a red light recklessly may intend the action (driving fast) but not the harm — still not malice. But someone who tampers with a colleague's work specifically to ruin their career? That is malice in full form.

It helps to draw clear lines:

  • Malice ≠ Anger. Anger is an emotion — it flares up and fades. Malice is more calculated and lasting. You can be furious at someone without bearing them malice. Malice often has a coolness to it; it can survive long after the heat of anger has passed.
  • Malice ≠ Hatred. Hatred is a feeling. Malice is the active desire to do something about that feeling — to see the person hurt. Hatred can sit inside you quietly; malice reaches outward.
  • Malice ≠ Indifference. Malice requires you to care enough about a person to want their suffering. Pure indifference — not caring whether someone is hurt — is not malice.
  • Malice ≠ Spite. These are close cousins, but spite is usually smaller in scale — a petty, almost childish desire to hurt someone as a reaction ("I'll ruin her party just to see her upset"). Malice is deeper, more serious, and more intentional. All spite has a touch of malice; not all malice is spite.

Malice is not always the same intensity. It can range across a spectrum:

At one end: A quiet, simmering wish that someone would fail — hoping bad things happen to a person you resent. This is malice in a passive sense. You haven't done anything yet, but the intention is there.

In the middle: Spreading false rumors about someone to damage their reputation, or sabotaging a coworker's project — deliberate harmful actions driven by that hostile intent.

At the far end: Taking careful, premeditated steps to cause serious harm to another person — physical, financial, or otherwise.

This is where the word carries its most precise and serious weight. In law, malice does not just mean "being mean." It has a very specific meaning that can determine whether someone is guilty of a crime and how severe the punishment is.

Malice in criminal law generally refers to the mental state of a person who commits a crime — specifically, that they intended to do harm or acted with reckless disregard for human life or safety.

"Malice aforethought" is a famous legal phrase. "Aforethought" means thought out in advance. So "malice aforethought" means the person planned the harmful act before doing it — they didn't just snap; they thought it through. This is central to defining murder (as opposed to manslaughter, which lacks this premeditated intent). When a prosecutor says a killing was done with malice aforethought, they are saying: the killer meant to kill, planned it, and was not acting out of sudden passion or accident.

There are also two subtypes in law:

  • Express malice: the person explicitly intended the harmful outcome (e.g., "I want to kill him" — and then they do).
  • Implied malice: the person didn't necessarily plan a specific harm, but acted in such a dangerously reckless way that the law treats it as if they intended the consequences (e.g., firing a gun randomly into a crowd — even without a specific target in mind, the recklessness implies malice).

In civil law (lawsuits between people, not criminal cases), malice matters too. For instance, in defamation cases (when someone lies about you and damages your reputation), proving that the person acted with "actual malice" — meaning they knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true or false — can be critical to winning the case and receiving higher damages.
Common Phrases and How They're Used

• "With malice" — done deliberately and with hostile intent. "He sabotaged her presentation with malice."
  • "Without malice" — done without any intention to harm; accidentally or innocently. "She criticized his work without malice — she just wanted to help."
  • "Bear malice toward someone" — to hold a persistent ill will or wish of harm against a person. "After all these years, she still bears malice toward her former business partner."
  • "Out of malice" — motivated purely by the desire to harm. "He spread those rumors out of malice, not because he believed them."
  • "Malice aforethought" — premeditated harmful intent (primarily legal; see above).
  • "With malice toward none" — a famous phrase from Abraham Lincoln meaning: without hostility or desire for revenge against anyone. It is often quoted to signal forgiveness or a generous spirit.
The Feeling of Malice from the Inside

If you try to imagine what malice feels like from the perspective of the person who holds it:

There is a target — a specific person (or group) they resent, fear, envy, or hate. And there is a want — a real desire to see that person fail, suffer, or be destroyed. It can feel almost like satisfaction in the idea of the other person's pain. Crucially, the person with malice is not indifferent — they are invested in the harm happening. They may plan, wait, and act carefully to ensure it does.

This is why malice is morally considered one of the darker human qualities. It is not impulsive or accidental — it is chosen.
Malice is the deliberate, intentional desire to cause harm or suffering to someone, driven by ill will — not accident, not impulse, but a cold and knowing wish that another person be hurt.
10143:
Malicious means having a strong, deliberate desire to harm, hurt, or cause damage to someone — and often taking pleasure or satisfaction in doing so.

If someone does something malicious, they are not acting by accident, not acting carelessly, and not acting with good intentions that went wrong. They are acting with the specific, conscious goal of causing pain, damage, or trouble to another person.

To truly understand this word, you need to see that it rests on three ideas working together:

1. Intent — the harm is on purpose.
This is the most important part. A person who accidentally knocks over your glass of water is not malicious. A person who deliberately knocks it over to ruin your work is. The word "malicious" is impossible without intention. The person chose to cause harm.

2. Ill-will — there is a dark feeling behind the act.
Malicious behavior doesn't come from a cold, neutral place. It comes from a place of spite, hatred, cruelty, or deep resentment toward someone. The person genuinely wants bad things for you. This inner feeling — this wish for someone to suffer — is called malice, and "malicious" is simply the adjective form of that noun.

3. A sense of pleasure or satisfaction in the harm caused.
A truly malicious person is not reluctant about the harm they cause. They often enjoy it, or at least feel deeply satisfied by it. This is what separates malicious behavior from, say, a difficult decision that hurts someone but is made out of necessity.
The Spectrum: What Is and Isn't Malicious

Understanding what a word does not mean is just as important as understanding what it does mean.

Not malicious:

  • A surgeon causes you pain during an operation. → The intent is to help you, not hurt you. Not malicious.
  • A driver accidentally hits another car. → It was an accident, not deliberate. Not malicious.
  • A manager gives you harsh feedback about your work. → If it's honest and well-meaning, not malicious — even if it stings.
  • A person lies to protect someone's feelings. → No desire to harm. Not malicious.

Malicious:

  • Someone spreads false rumors about you at work specifically to get you fired. → Deliberate, spiteful, harmful. Malicious.
  • A person secretly deletes your important files on a computer to sabotage your project. → Intentional damage with clear ill-will. Malicious.
  • A classmate mocks you in front of others not because it's funny, but because they want to see you feel humiliated. → Cruel intent. Malicious.

The key question to ask yourself is: "Did this person act this way because they wanted to cause harm?" If yes, it's malicious.

"Malicious" is not a light or casual word. It is strong and serious. It implies a real, deep wish to harm — not a moment of thoughtlessness or rudeness. When you call someone's actions malicious, you are making a significant claim: that they acted from a place of genuine ill-will, with full awareness of what they were doing.

This is why the word appears frequently in legal and formal contexts. In law, "malicious" is used to describe acts done with no legitimate reason, purely to cause harm — such as malicious prosecution (filing a lawsuit purely to harass someone) or malicious damage (deliberately destroying someone's property).

Malicious intent — the deliberate plan to cause harm. Courts often ask whether someone acted with malicious intent.

Malicious gossip — rumors or talk spread not out of curiosity but specifically to damage someone's reputation.

Malicious attack — an assault, whether physical or digital, carried out with the goal of causing serious harm.

Malicious software (malware) — computer programs designed specifically to damage, steal from, or take control of someone's system without their knowledge.

A malicious smile — a smile that is not warm or friendly, but rather one that signals the person is enjoying your misfortune or is plotting something harmful.

If you want to feel the meaning of this word rather than just know it intellectually, think of a villain in a story. Not a villain who does harm because they're desperate, or confused, or afraid — but one who enjoys causing suffering, who plans it, who delights in it. That quality — that dark, deliberate, pleasure-in-harm — is exactly what "malicious" captures.
Malicious = deliberately wanting to hurt or harm someone, driven by ill-will, and often with a sense of satisfaction in doing so.
10144:
Malign means evil, harmful, or having a deeply threatening influence. When you call something malign, you are saying it is not just unpleasant or mildly bad — you are saying it carries a dark, injurious quality, often with a sense that harm is being done deliberately or is baked into the very nature of the thing.

Think of it as two ideas fused into one word: evil + harmful. A malign thing doesn't just accidentally hurt you — it hurts you because something sinister is at the core of it.

The adjective "malign" is almost always used to describe abstract things — forces, influences, intentions, presences, spirits, effects. You wouldn't typically call a physical object malign, but you absolutely would call a force or intention malign.

Here are the kinds of things "malign" commonly describes, with an example for each:

Influence — "She felt a malign influence had taken hold of the boy, slowly turning him cruel and dishonest."
Here, the influence is portrayed as something evil that is actively working to corrupt someone.

Forces — "The soldiers believed malign forces were working against them, as if fate itself wanted them to fail."
"Malign forces" is a very common pairing. It suggests dark, sinister powers — sometimes supernatural, sometimes just deeply hostile circumstances.

Intent / Purpose — "His smile was warm, but his intent was entirely malign — he wanted to destroy her reputation."
A person can have a malign purpose: they look harmless on the surface, but their goals are evil.

Spirit or Presence — "The villagers feared a malign spirit haunted the forest."
In folklore or supernatural contexts, a malign spirit is one that wants to harm, not help.

Effect — "Years of propaganda had a malign effect on the population, filling them with fear and suspicion."
Here, something (propaganda) produces a malign effect — damage that is deep and far-reaching.

Neglect or Power — "The malign neglect of the city's leaders left thousands in poverty."
This is a powerful usage. "Malign neglect" means the neglect is not just careless — it feels willful, even cruel.

This is a word with a dark, serious, almost ominous tone. It carries more weight than simply saying "bad" or "harmful." When a writer or speaker chooses "malign," they are signaling that the evil or harm involved is:

  • Deep-rooted, not shallow or accidental
  • Threatening, in a way that feels powerful and hard to escape
  • Often intentional, or at least inherent to the nature of the thing

Compare these three sentences:

  • "The drug had a bad effect on his health." — simple and plain
  • "The drug had a harmful effect on his health." — slightly more formal, still neutral
  • "The drug had a malign effect on his health." — this suggests the harm is serious, pervasive, perhaps even sinister

"Malign" is the strongest and most ominous of the three.

Malign vs. Harmful: "Harmful" simply describes something that causes damage — a rock falling on your foot is harmful. "Malign" implies a darker, more sinister quality. A rock can't be malign, but a person's deliberate cruelty can be.

Malign vs. Evil: "Evil" is a strong moral judgment about a person or act. "Malign" focuses more on the nature or effect of something — its corrupting, threatening, damaging quality. You can say a force is malign even when it's not a moral agent.

Malign vs. Malevolent: "Malevolent" specifically means wanting to do evil — it's about intention and desire. "Malign" is broader — it can describe things that are harmful by nature, not just things that consciously wish harm. A disease cannot be malevolent (it has no wishes), but its effects can be described as malign.

Malign vs. Malignant: These two are close cousins. "Malignant" is the more common medical word — you've likely heard "malignant tumor." Outside medicine, "malignant" also suggests something actively spreading and getting worse. "Malign" is more literary and is used to describe a general quality of evil or harm rather than something spreading.
Intensity: How Strong Is This Word?

Very strong. This is not a word you reach for to describe everyday annoyances or mild problems. You use "malign" when you want to convey that something is fundamentally, seriously, perhaps even darkly evil or harmful. It is a word that belongs in serious writing, literature, journalism about grave matters, or thoughtful speech. Using it casually for something trivial ("this traffic jam has a malign influence on my mood") would sound overdramatic or even humorous.

If someone asked you to define "malign" in one sentence, you could say:

Something is malign if it is evil or deeply harmful in nature, especially in a dark, threatening, or sinister way.

And if they asked for an example sentence that captures the word perfectly:

"Historians argue that the king's malign influence over the courts of justice led to decades of corruption and suffering for ordinary people."

Here you can see everything at work: the influence is not just bad — it is evil in character, it causes serious harm, and it reaches far and wide.

Once you understand that "malign" = evil + harmful + sinister in nature, you will recognize it instantly every time you encounter it, and you'll know exactly when it's the right word to choose.
10145:
To malign someone means to say false, unfair, or harmful things about them — especially to damage how others see them. When you malign a person, you are speaking badly about them in a way that hurts their reputation, and crucially, in a way they don't deserve.

Think of it as a combination of three things happening at once: speech + falsehood (or unfairness) + harm to someone's name.
Why "False or Unfair" Matters So Much

This is the heart of the word. Maligning is not the same as honest criticism. If your friend genuinely did something wrong and you tell people about it truthfully, that is not maligning. But if you exaggerate, twist the truth, or make things up entirely to make them look bad — that is maligning.

The word carries a strong sense of injustice. The person being maligned is almost always seen as a victim — someone who is being treated unfairly by words.

When someone maligns another person, they are usually talking to a third party — not directly to the person they're attacking. This is what separates it from an insult. An insult is thrown at someone's face. Maligning happens behind someone's back, or in public forums, or in the press — anywhere that shapes how others think of that person.

So the damage is reputational. The goal (whether conscious or not) is to make the world think less of that person.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Criticize — Criticism can be completely fair, honest, and even kind. Maligning is never fair.

Insult — An insult attacks a person directly. Maligning attacks a person's image in front of others.

Gossip — Gossip is sharing personal details (true or false) out of curiosity or entertainment. Maligning specifically aims to destroy a reputation.

Defame — Very close to malign, but "defame" is more of a legal/formal term. Malign is more literary and emotional.

Vilify — To vilify is to portray someone as outright evil or monstrous. It's an extreme version of maligning. All vilifying is maligning, but not all maligning is vilifying.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Malign" is a formal and somewhat literary word. You won't hear it in casual everyday chatter as much as you'd hear "badmouth" or "trash-talk." But it is very common in writing — journalism, literature, essays, and formal discussion.

It also carries moral weight. When you say someone was maligned, you are implicitly defending them. You are saying: this person did not deserve what was said about them. The word naturally takes the side of the victim.
A Very Common Phrase to Know

You will very often see "malign" used in the phrases "often maligned" or "much maligned." These phrases are used to describe someone or something that gets unfair criticism repeatedly. For example:

"The much-maligned athlete finally got a chance to prove his critics wrong."

This means: the athlete was constantly spoken of negatively and unfairly, and now he has a chance to show that the criticism was wrong.

• "She worked hard to build her career, only to be maligned by jealous rivals."

— She was a victim of unfair, damaging talk from people who envied her.

  • "He felt it was wrong to malign someone who wasn't present to defend themselves."

— He believed it was unjust to say harmful things about someone behind their back.

  • "The documentary maligned the scientist by leaving out key facts about his work."

— The documentary portrayed the scientist unfairly by omitting important truths.

  • "Stop maligning her — you don't even know her."

— A direct plea to someone to stop speaking badly and unfairly about another person.
To malign someone is to speak of them in a false or unfair way that harms their reputation — and the word always carries the feeling that the person being spoken about doesn't deserve it.
10146:
Malignance is the quality or state of being deeply, actively harmful — not in a mild or passing way, but in a way that is serious, dangerous, and often relentless. Something that has malignance doesn't just cause small trouble; it causes real, severe damage. And crucially, it seems driven toward that damage — as if destruction is baked into its very nature.

If harm existed on a scale from mild to extreme, malignance sits near the far end. It's not just "bad." It's aggressively, dangerously bad — the kind that is hard to stop and tends to spread or deepen.

1. General and Figurative Use — describing people, feelings, or forces

When used outside of medicine, malignance describes a profound quality of evil, hostility, or destructive intent in a person, an emotion, an influence, or even an abstract force.

Applied to a person, it doesn't merely mean they are unkind or selfish. It means their very character is bent toward causing harm to others — with depth and drive. There is something in them that doesn't just stumble into causing damage; it moves toward it.

Applied to a force — like hatred, a destructive ideology, or a cruel power — malignance says that force is not neutral. It actively corrodes, destroys, or poisons whatever it touches. It doesn't sit still.

  • "There was a malignance in his eyes that unsettled everyone around him." — His look wasn't just cold or unfriendly. It felt like a genuine threat, something dark and purposeful.
  • "The malignance of the regime's philosophy left generations scarred." — The philosophy wasn't merely wrong; it had a quality that relentlessly caused harm, ate away at people's lives.

2. Medical Use — describing disease, especially cancer

In medicine, malignance describes the quality that makes a disease — particularly a tumor — dangerous and life-threatening. A malignant tumor isn't just an abnormal growth; it has this specific dangerous character: it grows uncontrollably, invades surrounding healthy tissue, and can break off and travel to other parts of the body (a process called metastasis). It doesn't stay contained. It doesn't stop on its own.

When a doctor confirms the malignance of a tumor, they are saying: this growth has that dangerous, aggressive, spreading nature — as opposed to a benign tumor, which is relatively harmless because it stays in one place and does not invade or spread.

  • "Tests confirmed the malignance of the growth, and treatment began at once."
The Weight and Intensity of the Word

Malignance is a heavy word. It is not used lightly, because it signals something genuinely and gravely harmful. Consider the difference:

  • Someone being rude → not malignance
  • Someone being hateful → still not malignance
  • Something whose fundamental nature is deeply, relentlessly, dangerously destructive → that is malignance

Because of this weight, the word belongs to serious, careful language — literature, formal writing, medical reports, thoughtful essays. You will almost never hear it in casual conversation. When a writer or speaker reaches for "malignance," they are making a precise, deliberate statement: this is not ordinary harm. This is something deeply and fundamentally threatening.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Malice is about intent — the desire, held in a person's mind, to hurt someone. Malice lives in consciousness. Malignance is broader: it can describe the quality of things (like a disease) that have no mind or intent at all. A tumor doesn't have malice, but it absolutely has malignance.

Malevolence means wishing evil upon others — it's focused on the desiring side of harm. Malignance, again, is broader. It describes destructive force that is realized and actual, not merely wished for.

Malignancy is the more commonly used noun and is nearly identical in meaning to malignance. The key practical difference: malignancy can refer to both the quality itself and to a specific, concrete instance of it — a doctor can say "a malignancy was found," meaning an actual cancerous tumor. Malignance refers more purely to the quality or state in the abstract. In everyday use, especially in medicine, malignancy is the far more common form. Malignance tends to appear more in literary and philosophical writing.

• A person's character, gaze, or intentions
  • An emotion taken to a dangerous extreme (hatred, envy that destroys)
  • A force, ideology, or institution
  • A tumor or disease (medical use)
  • A presence or atmosphere (in literary writing: "a sense of malignance filled the room")

Malignance is the quality of being deeply and dangerously harmful — actively, relentlessly so. In the general sense, it describes the worst quality of evil or hostility in a person or force. In the medical sense, it describes the dangerous, spreading nature of a disease like cancer. It is always serious, always at the extreme end of harm, and always used with care and intention. When you encounter this word, you are being told: whatever this is, it is not merely unpleasant — it is genuinely, powerfully dangerous.
10147:
Malignant describes something that is deeply harmful by its very nature — and not just harmful in a passive, accidental way, but harmful in an active, spreading, and hard-to-stop way. Think of it as something that doesn't just hurt you once and stop — it keeps growing, spreading, and getting worse over time. There is an almost "intent to destroy" quality to whatever is called malignant.

The word lives in two worlds: medicine and general description of evil or harm.

This is where you will most often encounter this word. In medicine, malignant is the opposite of benign.

Here is the difference:

A benign tumor or growth is like a harmless houseguest. It stays in one room, doesn't bother anyone else, and can often be removed easily. It won't kill you on its own.

A malignant tumor is the opposite. It is dangerous because it:

  • Invades the tissue around it, like a fire spreading to neighboring rooms.
  • Spreads to distant parts of the body through the blood or lymph system (this process is called metastasis).
  • Destroys healthy cells and organs as it grows.
  • Gets progressively worse if left untreated.

In short, a malignant growth = cancer. When a doctor says a tumor is malignant, they are saying it is cancerous and poses a serious, life-threatening danger.

Examples:

  • "The biopsy confirmed that the lump was malignant."
  • "She was relieved to learn the growth was benign, not malignant."

Medical phrases you may see:

  • Malignant tumor — a cancerous tumor
  • Malignant melanoma — a dangerous and aggressive form of skin cancer
  • Malignant hypertension — an extremely severe and rapidly worsening form of high blood pressure (note: even outside of tumors, "malignant" is used in medicine to signal that a condition is dangerously severe and fast-moving)

Outside of medicine, malignant describes a person, force, influence, or feeling that is deeply evil, spiteful, or harmful — especially when that harmful quality seems to come from within, like it is part of their very nature.

This is a stronger and more literary word than simply "bad" or "harmful." It carries a sense of active malice — a will to cause destruction or suffering. It also often suggests something that is spreading or hard to contain, just like in its medical sense.

Examples:

  • "A malignant rumor spread through the town and destroyed his reputation."
  • "He had a malignant influence over the younger members of the group."
  • "There was a malignant look in her eyes — pure hatred."
  • "The dictatorship was a malignant force that infected every corner of society."

Notice how in each case, the harm is not just present — it is spreading and corrupting things around it.

Whether used in medicine or everyday life, something malignant tends to have these qualities:

Harmful by nature — Not harmful by accident. Malignancy is built into the very identity of the thing.

Progressive — It doesn't stay the same. It grows, worsens, or spreads over time.

Invasive — It crosses boundaries. It moves into territory where it shouldn't be.

Threatening to life or well-being — The stakes are high. Malignant things put something important at serious risk.
4. Degrees of Severity — Why This Word Feels Heavy

"Malignant" is not a mild word. It belongs to the upper tier of serious, alarming descriptors. Compared to related words:

  • Harmful — something causes damage. (Neutral, factual)
  • Dangerous — something poses a risk. (Warns of threat)
  • Virulent — something is extremely severe or infectious. (Strong, often medical)
  • Malignant — something is deeply harmful, actively spreading, and difficult to stop — with an almost intentional destructive quality. (Gravest level)

When someone uses "malignant," they are signaling that the situation is serious, not trivial.
5. A Few More Sentences to Cement It

• "The doctor removed the malignant tissue before the cancer could spread further."
  • "Social media can sometimes be a malignant force, spreading lies faster than they can be corrected."
  • "His malignant jealousy slowly poisoned every friendship he had."
  • "The investigation revealed a malignant corruption at the heart of the organization."
Malignant means actively harmful, dangerous, and spreading in a way that is deeply destructive — like cancer in the body, or like a deeply evil force in the world.
10148:
Malignity means a deep, powerful, and active quality of evil or intense ill will — either in a person's character, or in the dangerous nature of a disease.

Think of it this way: it is not just disliking someone or wishing them a bad day. It is a dark, ingrained, almost burning quality of wanting to cause serious harm or suffering — or, in a medical setting, the dangerous quality of a disease that makes it destructive and hard to stop.

The word is used in two distinct areas of life, and it's worth understanding both clearly.
Meaning 1: In Human Character and Behavior

When used to describe a person or their actions, malignity refers to a profound, deep-seated, and active ill will — a fundamental quality of evil that goes far beyond ordinary hatred or dislike.

It is not an emotion that flashes in the moment (like anger). It is a settled, enduring quality — almost as if the desire to harm is baked into a person's character. It implies that someone is not just capable of cruelty in a weak moment, but that cruelty and harmful intent are characteristic of who they are.

Example sentences:

  • "The malignity of his hatred drove him to destroy everything she had built."
  • "She saw pure malignity in his eyes — not just anger, but a cold, deep desire to ruin her."
  • "His malignity was not impulsive; it was patient, calculated, and relentless."

How Is It Different From Similar Words?

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise:

  • Dislike → you simply don't enjoy someone's company.
  • Hatred → a strong negative feeling toward someone.
  • Malice → a clear desire or intention to harm someone. More about a specific wish to cause harm.
  • Malignity → goes a step further than malice. It describes the quality or character of being deeply and fundamentally evil in intention. Where malice can sometimes be a momentary or specific desire, malignity suggests something more settled, more intense, and more constitutionally evil — almost a defining trait of a person rather than a passing feeling.

Think of it on a scale:

Annoyance → Dislike → Hatred → Malice → Malignity

Malignity sits at the extreme end. It is not a mood. It is a nature.

Also note: malignity is not passive. It is active. A person with malignity does not just silently wish harm — they act toward causing it.

In medical and scientific language, malignity refers to the quality of being malignant — that is, the degree to which a disease (especially a tumor or cancer) is dangerous, invasive, and life-threatening.

When doctors say a tumor has malignity, they mean it has the capacity to grow destructively, invade surrounding healthy tissue, spread to other parts of the body, and resist treatment. It is the opposite of benign (harmless or non-spreading).

Example sentences:

  • "The biopsy was performed to determine the malignity of the growth."
  • "The malignity of the cancer was rated high, indicating it was aggressive and fast-spreading."

In this context, malignity is not about evil feelings — it is purely about how destructive and dangerous a disease is by its very nature.

The word can be used in the plural — malignities — to refer to specific acts, instances, or expressions of malignant intent or behavior.

Example:

  • "History recorded all the malignities he committed against his own people."

Here, "malignities" refers to specific cruel or harmful acts — the individual expressions of a malignant character.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

Malignity is a formal and literary word. You will mostly find it in:

  • Classical and 19th-century literature (Shakespeare, Milton, Dickens, and similar writers used it often)
  • Formal essays, academic writing, and serious nonfiction
  • Medical and clinical writing (in the disease sense)
  • Legal or historical documents

It is rarely used in everyday casual conversation. If someone says it in speech, they are being deliberately formal, poetic, or emphatic.

Malignity is the deep, enduring, and active quality of being fundamentally harmful or evil — either referring to a person's settled character of intense ill will and cruelty, or to the dangerous, life-threatening nature of a disease.
10149:
To malinger means to pretend to be sick, injured, or unable to function — or to deliberately exaggerate a real illness — in order to get out of a duty, responsibility, or obligation you simply don't want to do.

The person doing it is not actually as sick as they claim (or not sick at all). They know this. It is a conscious, calculated act of deception.

Think of it in three parts:

1. There is faking or exaggerating involved.
The malingerer either invents an illness entirely, or takes a minor real symptom and blows it wildly out of proportion. Either way, the suffering they present to the world is not genuine.

2. The faking is intentional.
This is crucial. The person knows they are doing it. They are not confused, not delusional, not mistaken about their own health. They are making a deliberate choice to deceive.

3. There is a goal — usually avoidance.
The malingerer wants to escape something: a military assignment, a hard day at work, an exam, a legal obligation, a difficult task. The fake illness is the tool they use to get out of it.

• A soldier who develops a sudden "mystery back pain" right before his unit is sent to a dangerous combat zone — and the pain disappears the moment the deployment is cancelled — is malingering.
  • An employee who calls in sick every single Monday, but is actually fine and just wants a longer weekend, is malingering.
  • A student who clutches her stomach and moans on the morning of a big exam she hasn't studied for, convincing her parents she's too ill to go to school, is malingering.
  • Someone who had a minor car accident and genuinely sprained their wrist, but then tells every doctor that they cannot move their entire arm and are in unbearable, constant pain — far beyond what the injury actually causes — in order to receive a larger insurance payout, is also malingering. Exaggerating a real symptom counts just as much as inventing a fake one.

• "The doctor suspected the patient was malingering when his symptoms vanished the moment he heard he wouldn't have to testify in court."
  • "She had been malingering for weeks, calling in sick while secretly enjoying her time at home."
  • "His commanding officer knew he was a malingerer the moment he saw him walking perfectly normally off duty."
What Makes Malingering Different From Similar Things

This is where a lot of people get confused, so this section is important.

Malingering vs. Being Genuinely Sick
Someone who is truly ill and stays home from work is not malingering. The single most defining feature of malingering is intent. A sick person isn't choosing to feel bad. A malingerer is choosing to claim they feel bad. Remove the conscious intent, and you no longer have malingering.

Malingering vs. Hypochondria (Illness Anxiety)
A hypochondriac genuinely, sincerely believes they are seriously ill, even when doctors say they're fine. They are not lying — they are convinced. A malingerer, by contrast, knows perfectly well they are not sick. One is a matter of delusion or anxiety; the other is a matter of deception. This is a sharp and important difference.

Malingering vs. Factitious Disorder (also called Munchausen Syndrome)
This is the trickiest comparison. In factitious disorder, a person also fakes or induces illness — but their motive is psychological: they crave the care, sympathy, and attention that comes with being a patient. They want to be a sick person. A malingerer, on the other hand, doesn't want to be sick for its own sake — they just want to use the sick role to dodge something specific. The malingerer wants the benefit (avoiding work, getting money). The factitious patient wants the identity (being cared for). Different goals, same act of deception.

"Malinger" is not a neutral word. It carries a distinctly negative and accusatory tone. When you call someone a malingerer, you are accusing them of being lazy, dishonest, and manipulative. It is not a gentle word. You would use it when you believe someone is genuinely exploiting the sympathy of others or abusing a system.

It shows up most commonly in three settings:

  • The military — where avoiding duty has serious consequences and is taken very seriously
  • Medicine and law — where doctors, insurance companies, or courts need to determine whether someone is truly injured or faking
  • Everyday language — to describe anyone who is transparently dodging responsibilities under a fake pretence of illness
One-Sentence Summary to Lock It In
To malinger is to deliberately fake or exaggerate illness in order to avoid a duty or obligation — knowing full well that you are not as sick as you claim.
